lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- The Weekend That Actually Happened
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Janderson Roberto Teixeira | Lesson 2 -- The Weekend That Actually Happened
lesson.grammar_point: past simple, regular and irregular verbs

listenings.text: Hi, it is me. Listen, I have to tell you about Saturday, because it did not go to plan at all. We booked a table for one o'clock at that place by the market. We arrived at five past one and the restaurant was closed. Closed on a Saturday. So we walked to the square instead, and it was so crowded that we gave up after ten minutes. In the end we bought bread and cheese and we sat in the park on our own for two hours, and honestly it was the best afternoon I had all month. Anyway, call me back. I want to hear what you did.

Last year I took eleven days off and I did not travel once. People kept asking me where I went, and the honest answer was nowhere. I stayed at home, I caught up on about forty things, and I finished two books I started in twenty twenty-four. The first three days were terrible. I felt guilty and I checked my email far too often. Then something changed. By the second week I stopped looking at the phone in the morning, I walked somewhere new every afternoon, and I ended up knowing my own neighbourhood better than I did after fifteen years of living in it. It was not a holiday. It turned out to be something better.

extra_audio.text: Claire asks Janderson how his weekend was. He answers that it was quiet, and that he did not do very much on Saturday. Claire asks whether he went anywhere on Sunday. He says he took his daughter to a museum nearby, and that it was completely crowded. Claire asks whether it was worth it, and he says the queue was long but his daughter loved it.

reading.rtitle: The Saturday That Did Not Go to Plan
paras: I had one day off in three weeks, so I planned it carefully. I booked a table for lunch, I found a small museum nearby, and I wrote the whole thing down on Friday night like a man who was afraid of wasting it.

None of it worked. The restaurant closed for a private party and nobody called me. The museum was so crowded that the queue went around the corner, and after twenty minutes standing in the sun I gave up and walked away. By half past one I was hungry, annoyed, and completely on my own in a part of the city I did not know.

So I took a shortcut through a street I had never seen before, and I ended up in a small square with four tables outside a bakery. I sat there for two hours. I ate a sandwich, I read half a newspaper, and I did not look at my telephone once. Nobody knew where I was and nobody needed me.

It turned out to be the best day I had all month, and I did not plan a single minute of it. I am not saying that plans are useless. I am saying that the day I organised disappeared by lunchtime, and the day I did not organise is the one I still remember.
reading.source: Article -- a weekend column in a city newspaper

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Restaurants and museums are usually badly organised at the weekend
The carefully planned day fell apart, and the unplanned part of it turned out to be the good part
You should never book a table in advance
